title: The US Just Proposed a 12.5% Tariff on India Over Forced Labour. Trade Talks in Delhi Are Still Going.
excerpt: Washington's Section 301 investigation names India among 54 economies without a forced-labour import ban. The timing — mid-negotiation — is not a coincidence.
body:
The United States Trade Representative has proposed an additional 12.5 percent tariff on imports from India, accusing it of failing to curb imports made with forced labour. The announcement landed on Tuesday, the second day of three-day trade talks in New Delhi between Indian officials and a U.S. delegation led by Assistant USTR Brendan Lynch.

The proposal is part of a sweeping Section 301 investigation that targets 60 economies accounting for more than 99 percent of U.S. imports. A 92-page report from the USTR concluded that India's approach to forced-labour imports is "unreasonable" and a "burden on U.S. commerce."

"The failure of our most important trading partners to address the importation of goods made with forced labour is unacceptable," USTR Jamieson Greer said in a statement. "This creates a dynamic where American workers are forced to compete globally on an unlevel playing field."

## Two Tiers of Tariffs

The USTR divided the 60 economies into two groups. Six nations — Canada, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan, and Ecuador — have some form of forced-labour import prohibition in place and face a proposed 10 percent additional duty for not enforcing it effectively. The remaining 54 economies, including India, China, Japan, South Korea, and Australia, lack such a prohibition entirely and face the steeper 12.5 percent rate.

The proposed duties will not take effect immediately. The USTR has opened a public comment period through July 6, with hearings scheduled for July 7. But the timeline is tight. A new tariffs architecture under Section 301 is set to take effect on July 24, following the Supreme Court's February ruling that struck down President Trump's earlier reciprocal tariffs as unconstitutional.

## The Trade Talks in Delhi

The timing is deliberate. India and the United States have been negotiating the first phase of a bilateral trade agreement since February. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said on June 1 that about 99 percent of discussions for the first tranche had been completed. The U.S. delegation, led by chief negotiator Brendan Lynch, arrived in Delhi for a three-to-four-day session that is meant to finalise the broad contours before USTR Greer's expected visit to India in July.

According to sources tracking the negotiations, the U.S. has proposed locking India into an 18 percent tariff rate under the bilateral framework — a rate it is pitching as insulation against potentially higher Section 301 levies. India wants a guarantee that whatever rate it accepts will remain lower than those imposed on competing developing economies like Vietnam, Bangladesh, and Malaysia. Without that competitive edge, officials argue, the deal becomes politically and economically unjustifiable.

## India's Response

India has rejected the forced-labour allegations. According to Bloomberg, New Delhi has urged Washington to terminate the investigation, calling the findings misplaced. Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative, pointed out that the USTR investigation was not about forced labour in Indian exports but about whether India blocks imports tied to forced labour from elsewhere — a distinction that could form the basis of a legal challenge.

India's commerce ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans and NRIs watching the trade relationship, the forced-labour tariff is a new pressure point in a negotiation that already has several. Indian textile, pharmaceutical, and IT exports to the United States — sectors that employ millions and sustain family remittance networks — could face higher costs if the tariffs take effect. The bilateral trade agreement is meant to prevent exactly this scenario, but the window to finalise it is narrowing. Greer's visit in July will likely determine whether the deal gets done before the new tariffs kick in.

The European Union has already called the findings "utterly absurd." But for India, the stakes are different. Its trade surplus with the U.S. was $45.7 billion in 2025. Washington sees that surplus as leverage. New Delhi sees it as proof that the relationship works. The next four weeks will test which framing wins.

*Sources: Reuters, Financial Times, The Hindu BusinessLine, The Indian Eye, Outlook Business*
author: Diaspora Desk
